segments.text: Welcome, and
welcome to people that are now watching us.
We are talking about the Financial Markets International
Money Transfer Amendment Bill, which is a member's bill in the name
of Arena Williams, and she is now at the table, and we have 15
minutes with you. That's inclusive of question time, so I will hand
to you.
Thank you, Madam Chair. I will leave plenty of time for questions.
But colleagues,
this is a funny setup, and I thought I would take just a minute to tell you why
I've asked governance and administration to take this on as a piece of work,
why we find ourselves here with a member's
bill to deal with an issue which MBIE has provided advice on to four
successive commerce ministers, beginning with the Honorable Dr.
David Clark,
followed by the Honorable Duncan Webb, the Honorable Scott Simpson,
and now the current commerce minister.
And then finally, I'll leave you with some remarks about why
this issue is a real-world issue. It is one that began with a
constituent case for me in 2023,
and will remain something which affects all of us, not
only as electorate MPs, but as representatives and advocates for the diverse
communities within New Zealand who use these services, and the vulnerable
consumers who are disproportionately affected by these high costs
that New Zealanders pay. So to begin,
why do we find ourselves here? Because the regime that manages
international money transfers and their costs in some jurisdictions has a natural
home, a natural regulator, but because we find ourselves with a sort of Twin
Peaks regulation system, where we have a
banking regulator, financial services from the financial markets,
we also have MBIE looking across these sorts of products,
and primarily concerned with this sort of product because it is something that
consumers should be able to see the ticket price and pay the ticket price.
And then we also have international arrangements,
where it is important that we get our settings right in New
Zealand so that consumers who are making these transfers in New
Zealand, say to a bank account in the Pacific, have
transparency, and so that other jurisdictions that
work with us and are the main recipients or the main
contributors are getting a fair deal.
So there's no one regulator who's responsible for this issue.
I think this is an issue where we need greater transparency
so that the rules are fair for everyone, and that's why I've asked you to take a
look under the hood. It doesn't necessarily sit with EPC, it doesn't necessarily
sit with EDZ.
This is something which affects every New Zealander at least a few
times a year, but for some people every week when they are sending their
wages overseas to family members.
So why is this something which successive governments have had a crack at
and haven't been able to land? And this is a matter of public record,
your question about, is there a problem?
Yes, successive commerce ministers have thought this is a problem.
It's not only National ministers who have been asked
to have a look at this, it's also Labor ministers, but it is something that has
sort of fallen through the cracks of who is responsible for it.
The total size of the transfer market in New Zealand at
the end of this decade will be close to a billion dollars just in
the fees that we pay. About half of those are small business
and business fees, and then the other half includes a good whack
of consumer fees, around $200 million off the top of my
head, that ordinary people like you and me are paying on top of what
we would be paying if we were in a more competitive market like the UK or like the
EU. So that is a net drag on not only New Zealand's
productivity, but also on the price that consumers pay that's not going back into
their mortgages, it's not going back into their car loans, it's not going back into
those things that help them with the cost of living and make sure
that they can pay their bills at the end of the week.
Who does this primarily affect? Well,
you might imagine that we're talking here about workers who are making
payments every week and every fortnight. That is true.
The majority of these people who are hit by these larger fees
are also people with either English as a second language barriers, or people who
see transfer companies in the street,
who are advertising to them that there is a zero fee or
0% fee. And so in New Zealand, they are not entitled to
rely on that claim. But though they are being advertised a 0%
fee, those people who are paying their wages every week are actually paying quite a
large fee, and by the end of the year, they might be paying $2,000 to
$4,000 for a minimum wage worker
in that 0% fee.
But we're also talking about people who are booking holidays, booking
experiences, booking things in New Zealand currency where they're
going on a trip or a holiday. We're also talking about people who are migrating.
A
woman in my last public meeting about this told me that in her move from the
Philippines to New Zealand, she was caught in this and lost more than
$10,000, which she felt like she just didn't want to quite pass out
through about how much money that was for her when she was
making the biggest transfer she will ever make, the biggest investment to move
to a new country, to open a new business here,
because she felt like it was such a big investment and a
pretty humiliating one for her. We're also talking about people who
are older. Older New Zealanders are
more likely to be using these services and not alternatives,
which
offer a more competitive rate, because the most competitive
options in the New Zealand market right now are New Zealand startups.
They're New Zealand tech entrepreneurs who are seeing an opportunity right here
because the margin is so big that if you are a young New
Zealand tech hopeful, you can build a business that competes with
the banks, that competes with those transfer companies in the street,
and even if you've invested a few thousand dollars of your own money, you can make
something and with not a big company And not a big
customer base, you can actually make some money because the opportunity there
is so large because these margins have not been competed
down over time. This is a clear use of market power
where the largest incumbents have used their market size to
keep those big margins high.
This is something where I'm sure that my colleagues who have been briefed
on this before by officials would be frustrated by the briefing
that the committee has received, because that is the information that ministers
have received the last 10 years, but this still remains a problem.
And it remains a problem because those margins remain high.
There's not a clear regulating, and the rules that I have
proposed in my member's bill put the regulation-making power with the
regulator, with me. I have not proposed that this committee should
come up with a definition of what is a fair margin.
I have not suggested to you a cap. I have not suggested to you a regime which
requires the sorts of information that will be displayed.
I have simply suggested to you that you should give a regulation-making power
to the regulators, because that is the appropriate role for this parliament, and
that they should come up with the rules which are clear, and so everyone has a fair
playing field. My suggestion would be that the rules should make
everyone use the same sorts of disclosure that the apps have to use
already. Because we are seeing a growth in that market for New Zealanders, that
more and more people are switching to financial
apps and online services that are either New Zealand-based startups or
that are international competitors with our banks.
And that the fact that they can do it says to me that everyone
should be doing it, and that everybody in New Zealand should be able to get
the same fair deal that the people who are tech-savvy,
they're diligent, they're watching their money, they're well-informed,
wealthy people, are able to access by
using those services. I just want that for everyone.
So happy to take questions about the-
Okay, thank you. We've about six minutes for questions.
So Melissa, I'll start with you.
Thank you. Thank you for your submission.
Two questions in related to the example that you gave.
One is actually regarding the Filipino who was actually-
Yes
... migrating. You were talking about losing $10,000.
Yes.
So, what
is that fee for, and where did that fee go to?
Yeah.
Is one question. The other one is, you talked about when people are transferring
money,
the charge, they're actually paying a fee of $1,000.
Yeah.
So similar question.
What is the charge?
Where is the charge?
Yeah.
Who's actually taking it, and what percentage is it?
Great points. Okay. So, in this particular example, we
can work it through. There are four transactions that this woman made,
and they had to be at different times because of different points at which she was
able to sell her assets. She sold a couple of properties, and she also sold her
business, and she was then buying in New Zealand a mix of assets and
money in a bank account. So each transfer
for her had a slightly different rate, and two of them had a fee.
Was it through a bank?
Two were through a bank, and one was through a service.
And-
What service?
One of the services that she used was an app for her cash, and
that had a very low fee, and that fee was disclosed to her.
Was it Wise or PayPal or something else?
Not sure. I think it was one of the bigger ones, like I think it might've been
Zoom.
But not quite sure. She didn't tell me, but she-
Right
... it's also quite hard to get that specific information out of people because
they don't want to pass it out. But she did use one service, which was a low fee.
Then she used another service
once she was basically
at the point of buying a business,
and that
also,
the point of that was that there was a big fee attached to that one that
was also visible to her, but a large fee that she couldn't get out
of, which ended up being about $2,000, just the fee.
So it was added on to the transaction-
Added on to the transaction
... or is she taken out from her money?
Added on to the transaction.
Right.
The two next ones,
those were the ones with the foreign effects spread, where it was a
product which was advertised to her as a 0% fee,
but in the foreign exchange spread,
the RBNZ rate for the New Zealand dollar would be set
here, a transfer rate was set
here.
So within that, there was a margin that her transfer company was
making that was not disclosed to her first.
They would've been advertising that the New Zealand dollar was here,
when really New Zealand dollars were available to consumers like her at this
price. And that's the margin which this bill seeks to
regulate. It doesn't seek to regulate the two first kinds of fees,
because those were disclosed to her.
But in the second two transactions, which added
up to be fees of about $6,500 for
her, those are the fees that this bill's seeking to sort out.
And I'm not trying to sort it out for
our entire banking relationships, say, around the Asia-Pacific.
I'm just trying to sort it out here in New Zealand, because New
Zealand-based Filipinos who are making those
transactions to the Philippines are paying more
in the New Zealand market. The margins are huge in the New Zealand
market, because we haven't had any degree of
competition around those sorts of
transfer services. We're just getting to the stage.
And to invite more of that competition, we have to give them an even playing
field, or else
that competition that we're enjoying now where we're seeing new entrants coming
into the market, they will also be able to charge higher and higher
prices. We have to get our regulatory settings right so everyone comes down to a
competitive price.
Okay, thank you. Tim.
Yeah, just can I just ask two questions?
So you-
You kind of addressed it, but not really. Sorry, there's two parts to it.
So, one is
why it's at GNA. And I understand you said, well, that's not quite FSE,
it's not quite economic development, but it's definitely not GNA, right?
Because the FMA never reports here, MBIE never reports here.
We never deal with these kind of issues. So why has it come here?
I'm really passionate about sorting this out as a broader issue
for our relationships within the Pacific corridors, within, and
comparing ourselves to jurisdictions that we like to compare ourselves to, like
Australia, like the UK. We should have a regime which is most
similar to the governance arrangements within those countries.
We cannot reorganize the regulators to have a
stronger look at the sorts of prices that we put on financial products,
but we can make sure that we've got the right responsibility at this level.
That's why the regulation-making power,
I also considered sending it to the committee, which is the
expert committee for regulations, the Relations Review Committee,
because all I'm asking for is a new regulation-making power.
So in terms of the legislative design of this, nothing is subject matter
expert. Everything is the way that Parliament would delegate to a regulator.
But
I still don't hear why GNA. I get there's a
Pacific bit, maybe that's foreign affairs, I don't know.
There's a regulation-
Could be foreign affairs, could be regs, yeah
... but I haven't heard anything that, like it's not
DIA, it's not NEMA, it's not
local government, it's not any of the places that this committee deals
with. I'm just
trying to understand why-
You're right. There are several committees that this could have-
We need to move on because we haven't got much time, so-
Okay. So the other part was, can you just tell us why previous ministers
from whatever party, Duncan, whomever, why weren't they able to do
this?
It's something which has come up in, say, the COFI
regime, which is about consumer care and the expectations we have on
banks, financial institutions.
It's in the weeds of the regulation-making
powers, and yet we still don't have a regulation that is specific
around this.
they could have done it, just didn't hit the priority level
I think if we were having this discussion in 2019 and in
2022 when the lid was off COFI,
you might have also received advice, and ministers certainly did,
that we would have seen a tapering off of this in
New Zealand's market because the rules also
require fair dealing, pricing transparency of other sorts of
products,
that the powers already exist, and
that we would have seen market practice evolve
to...
It's in the shades of gray, and governments have
gone darker and darker gray in the specificity around this.
But this is the first time we've considered a specific requirement on
the regulator to implement rules around this.
Didn't you say it went to David Clark?
We're not going to get there now, sorry, because-
Okay
... we've run out of time, and I'm sorry about that.
We do have some other questions, but maybe members can actually get those to you
directly in that-
Yep
... article.
Cool. Thank you.
So we're actually opening now for submissions, and the first submission was the
Peanut Butter Collective, please. Hello, Paul.
And,
I'm going to hand over, but Paul, I haven't seen you for a long time, so
it's wonderful to see you.
Yeah. Thank you, Jane, Madam Chair, and members of the committee.
And I'm going to move, Jane.
I did have the pleasure of visiting Jane at a school many years ago-
Yes, yeah
... when I was a public servant, and haven't had much to do with her since, but-
I know
... to follow you on the news.
And unfortunately, I have to leave now, but-
Okay
... yeah. But it's lovely to see you. Yeah.
I also have a good friend from the Philippines.
She lives here in New Zealand and regularly sends money back to support her
parents. She has a business degree.
She works in the finance industry here in New Zealand.
She shops around for a good rate, and yet she was
surprised by the evidence my research turned up and what she's
paying in margins
within the exchange rate component not easily visible for her.
I guess I see that if somebody as capable as
she can't make the right decisions with that background, then
it's not a failure of the consumer or of the shopper, but there's
something else that's broken here in the system.
I'm Paul Seiler, I'm the co-founder of the Peanut Butter Collective.
We're a pre-revenue startup looking to apply data
method transparency of ruthless honesty to help Kiwi households get better
deals on life's essentials.
This bill came up in an environmental scan for me of what's happening.
There's a high mission overlap and zero business plan
overlap. So we're here based on evidence and method, nothing to do
with self-gain, nor lived harm, actually.
I personally don't send much money anywhere else.
To us, the problem is one that the fee
paid to remit money has two components. One is visible up front.
It might be zero, or it might be a number different.
The other is hidden within the exchange rate margin.
This is often not visible at the point of making a transaction and makes
comparison very difficult.
On the New Zealand Tonga corridor,
the World Bank data shows that the average rate for the fee
is around about 8%, including both components, but the range is what's
interesting. From about 17% for the main banks, with quite a low
spread around that number, down to 3% for the newer
fintech-like products.
The difference was quite alarming to me and kind of reinforces what the Commerce
Commission found, that the pricing is opaque and poorly understood.
So Peanut Butter Collective supports the bill, and we ask for a number of
changes. Only two I'll speak to here.
The first is that the binding minimum includes the fee that is
disclosed and the margin within the exchange rate, that those two are
locked together and made transparent so shoppers can make informed choices.
The second, we believe that the duty-
Should follow the activity of sending money so that it reaches all providers that
undertake this activity, not limited to only banks, insurers, or deposit
takers who might be the natural place this would
fall in the way that it's currently written.
We see this as a small bill that could
make a real difference for competition and for families.
I'm happy to take your questions.
Yeah, Le Manea.
Thank you for your submission. It's really helpful to try and
understand issues. And I'm really concerned about hearing
what you've provided here in terms of consumers having a
very clear suite of options and then understanding you could either be
front-loaded or not. It's really helpful.
And this is a problem in our community, because I'm talking to people every week,
who send remittances back home because they have their own obligations, whether
it's Pacific or ethnic.
The question I wanted to ask was, in terms
of the
range of, so you've outlined in your example, there was a
front-load cost of 17%, but it's the range.
It's the range. So are you saying to the committee that,
in terms of the range, who actually decides the range, or is it
just so out there that it's up to each business to
charge that range without having to
inform the consumer?
Individual providers of the service choose their own
exchange rate. They have better information than most of their
customers in choosing that. I'm not seeking any regulation around
the exchange rate they choose. I believe that businesses should be able to make
that choice.
Sure.
But they should declare the divergence between a published
mid-rate
that all providers in the market use, certainly for the same channel,
and whatever rate they wish to charge.
That would get made visible upfront, in a standardized format,
so that shoppers, consumers can make a choice.
Just supplementary, Chair.
Please.
Just a supplementary on that. To declare that
even if English is a second language, because a lot of the people that I deal with,
you would actually go to a... Well, from what I can understand from local
examples, you would choose a provider or a
business that you've had really good feedback from
family or people in the community because there's that trusted
relationship.
So just in your point of declaration upfront,
that this is the cost. You're going to put in, for example,
$100, but there's these charges to be aware of.
So they've disclosed it right up front.
Mm-hmm.
So are you saying there's quite a mix in terms of businesses providing that
education for consumers?
There's no required disclosure. There's no standardized way of
conveying that, and providers act differently.
It would be difficult for any group of people,
any whanau or network, to make an informed decision, which others would
then follow based on trusted advice.
I'd just like the information to be transparent, comparable.
And then consumers, whether individual or larger groups, will make
informed decisions and
reward appropriate behaviors.
Thank you.
Andy Foster.
Yeah. Thank you very much, Paul. The question I wanted to ask is, these
organizations which are outside of COFI at the moment.
So I would've thought if you, there's a question, no, can't ask that.
A question I was interested in exploring was,
I would've thought it's an advantage from a, if I'm a consumer and
I see somebody who's being transparent about their fees,
I'd be more inclined to say I like that, as opposed to somebody who's opaque.
If the
organizations we're talking about remain opaque, then I would've
thought they would lose market share. People would tend to...
So I'm interested in your thoughts on that.
And secondly, you seem to be saying that the obligation attached, you

So, on the first question that you asked
about the reward for those who are
transparent or opaque.
Effectively, yes.
It's difficult to make fair comparisons when the numbers don't stack up.
The business might go to the organization who pitches zero fees, and that's a

It's just that the money that is recovered to run the cost of the service and any

I don't have a view really on whether opacity should be,
maybe I do. Opacity shouldn't be allowed to continue just because people might get
rewarded for being transparent when we could easily
solve the issue of
transparent for all comparable easily. Okay?
So the second part of the question.
On the COFI regime?
Yeah, which is, effectively if you're requiring, and this'll be something to
probably ask the officials later on, but,
if you're essentially, the COFI regime covers a certain range of
organizations. Doesn't cover another lot.
What you're kind of suggesting is that this arrangement covers both, and that
I don't know what that does to the architecture of the COFI regime.
I'm not an expert on that. It was the best home I could find for an obligation
that could apply with the lightest touch.
It is important not to force too high compliance costs on
smaller and lower margin operators because the corridors to Pacific
Islands have always been very shallow for capital flows.
It would be a shame if good work done here to increase
transparency and comparability penalized or forced out of
existence, the very providers who are challenging the established
high rates in providing alternative flows for currency.
Okay. We've got one minute left for Dr Shane Rickardson.
Thank you. You're proposing a baseline comparator, a margin
comparator. Just describe that a bit more.
In other regimes that have tackled this well ahead of ourselves, so
European Union, Singapore, Canada, England, United
States, they set a mid-market exchange rate
against which all rates used for one service are measured.
Who's they?
That differs by jurisdiction. It could be a central
agency of government. Some people have borrowed from international published
rates because the sheer number of
currency-to-currency combinations is very high.
That market rate is known, it can be published daily, and I do accept that rates
change within the day and there's allowance made in the details for how you could
deviate from that. But it's not saying that's the rate you must use, it's saying
that is the rate against which your currency exchange rate is measured.
The difference, I'm not saying with margin, as in I'm saying it's a
fee and margin, but it's part of the
cost to the consumer for using the service, and that it should be
added to the fee in a visible, easy to
calculate way, and then I or others make their decision about which remittance
service do I use.
Thanks, Paul. We're out of time there. Appreciate your time today.
We're going to move online to Wise, and I think we've got Jack
Pincheski
joining us.
Good morning.
Good morning. We've got 10 minutes for you.

Absolutely, Chair. Thank you so much. My name's Jack Pincheski.
I'm the APAC Government Relations Lead for Wise.
We're a global technology company that's building the best way to move and send
money around the world. And I should just start by saying Wise was
established on the basis of our
CEO founder, Kristo Käärmann, being frustrated by his inability
to send money overseas without being hit with hidden FX fees.
And we describe hidden FX fees as the differential between the
mid-market rate or the rate you'd see on Google, and the rate that

We are a fast-growing company. We've got 19 million people and businesses using us

Our business is the movement of money across borders.
We operate in New Zealand. We've established our New Zealand entity.

We are very excited about the prospect of this bill improving competition

We think that this bill will drive a large amount of competition in the

information that they need to make the best decision for themselves.
Currently, we see the regime for international money transfers as being opaque,

small businesses who may be using the least
cost-effective way to send money or receive money from overseas.

of years. We were speaking to the Commerce Commission about this as far

services. I'll
wind up by saying we endorse this bill.
We believe it will be a mechanism that will improve

to proceed.

they will go with trusted providers, but
the knowledge of choosing a provider is quite

community.

A person might choose an FX provider based on trust.

they're going to be highly motivated by cost.
The difficulty with the present situation is that a person sending money
is not aware of the full cost that would be
assessed to them
if they're not told the differential between a benchmark rate
and the FX rate, which is
charged to them by their bank or international money transfer provider.

For a person to make that decision,

of transmission. So we believe this bill, if
our recommendations on improving this bill are taken, we believe that that
will- Ensure that consumers will be able to see exactly what it is that
they're paying at the point of transmission, which may prompt
consumer switching behavior, which is one of the key parts of trying to

It would be a consumer switching from one provider who they deem to be too
expensive to another provider that they deem to be more suitable for their needs.

consumers to be able to go shopping, because
